title: The Lungs Take Over From the Placenta

scenes.tts: A fetus does not use its lungs to exchange gas, so where does its blood go? Researchers injected radioactive microspheres into fetal lambs and counted them organ by organ. Roughly forty to forty five percent of combined ventricular output went to the placenta. Under ten percent went to the lungs. Those are sheep numbers from an instrumented preparation, and human proportions are inferred from imaging.

Those are sheep numbers from an instrumented preparation, and human proportions are inferred from imaging.

scenes.tts: Three shunts route fetal blood past the liver and the lungs; the fetal lungs are fluid filled, with high resistance. The ductus venosus carries a variable share of the umbilical vein blood past the liver, toward the inferior vena cava. The foramen ovale, an opening in the atrial septum, passes a stream from the right atrium to the left. Most of the blood leaving the pulmonary artery crosses the ductus arteriosus into the aorta. Umbilical arteries carry blood back to the placenta, a low resistance bed in parallel with the fetal body.
scenes.visual: A schematic fetal circuit built piece by piece: placenta, umbilical vein, ductus venosus past the liver, foramen ovale between the atria, ductus arteriosus joining the pulmonary artery to the aorta, umbilical arteries back to the placenta.
scenes.narration: Three shunts route fetal blood past the liver and the lungs; the fetal lungs are fluid filled, with high resistance. scenes.tts: At birth, air fills the lungs and pulmonary vascular resistance falls. Pulmonary blood flow rises, and pulmonary venous return raises pressure in the left atrium. Once left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure, the flap of septum primum is pressed against the septum. The foramen ovale then stops carrying a right to left stream.
scenes.visual: Lung resistance drops, flow through the lungs grows, two atrial pressure gauges cross, and the flap at the foramen ovale closes against the septum.
scenes.narration: At birth, air fills the lungs and pulmonary vascular resistance falls. Pulmonary blood flow rises, and pulmonary venous return raises pressure in the left atrium. scenes.tts: Losing the placenta removes a low resistance circuit, so systemic vascular resistance and ventricular afterload rise. Oxygen constricts the ductus arteriosus, shown directly on fresh human ductal rings studied outside the body. These endpoints do not arrive together. In fifty healthy term neonates followed by ultrasound, the ductus arteriosus had closed in ninety four percent before day three. Only twelve percent had a closed ductus venosus by then, and Doppler found foramen ovale flow in every infant.

scenes.tts: Instrumented preterm lambs, six in each group, were clamped before ventilation or ventilated before clamping. Clamping first dropped mean right ventricular output by about sixty six percent. The group means fell from one hundred fourteen point six to thirty eight point eight millilitres per minute per kilogram. Heart rate fell about forty percent too. Ventilating first gave stable flows and pressures.

The group means fell from 114.6 to 38.8 mL/min/kg. Heart rate fell about 40 percent too. Ventilating first gave stable flows and pressures.
scenes.visual: Two timelines, clamp first and ventilate first; right ventricular output bars drop from 114.6 to 38.8 mL/min/kg in the first, stay stable in the second.

scenes.tts: The reading is that, before aeration, umbilical venous return supplies much of the filling of the left ventricle. This is a mechanism in preterm lambs, with no human outcome. The study cannot separate a transfusion of blood volume from preload replacement. Aeration lets pulmonary venous return take over the filling, so the order decides whether preload falls as afterload rises.
scenes.visual: Filling of the left ventricle switches source from umbilical venous return to pulmonary venous return, with the two limits written on screen.
